title: Superior vena cava obstruction
subtitle: The surgeon's role: tissue, airway caution, stent first

sources.title: Superior vena cava syndrome with malignant causes (Wilson LD, Detterbeck FC, Yahalom J)
Superior vena cava syndrome: a proposed classification system and algorithm for management (Yu JB, Wilson LD, Detterbeck FC)

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Lung cancer: diagnosis and management (NG122)

red_flags.text: Stridor, voice change or laryngeal oedema: airway compromise, the life-threatening presentation.
Confusion, reduced conscious level or headache worse on lying flat: cerebral oedema.
Syncope or hypotension, especially with a large anterior mediastinal mass compressing the heart or great vessels.
A request for a general anaesthetic for a biopsy in a patient with an anterior mediastinal mass and orthopnoea. Induction can cause complete airway or cardiovascular collapse.

do_now.text: Sit the patient up, give oxygen, and assess airway and neurological state. Severe symptoms need same-day oncology and interventional radiology input.
Life-threatening features (stridor, cerebral oedema, haemodynamic compromise): arrange urgent endovenous stenting, which relieves symptoms fastest, before a tissue diagnosis if necessary.
Without life-threatening features, avoid steroids until tissue is obtained: they can make lymphoma and thymoma undiagnosable.
Site IV access in the lower limb where possible; upper-limb veins drain into the obstructed system.

assess.text: Grade the severity: facial and arm swelling and venous distension at one end, laryngeal or cerebral oedema and haemodynamic compromise at the other.
Orthopnoea, positional dyspnoea and syncope: these predict collapse under anaesthesia and must be explicitly sought before any sedation.
Likely cause: lung cancer and lymphoma account for most malignant cases; consider germ cell tumour, thymoma and metastatic disease, and catheter or device-related thrombosis.
Performance status and whether the cancer is already diagnosed and staged.

investigate.text: CT chest with IV contrast to define the obstruction, the mass, collateral circulation, thrombus and the airway.
Tissue by the least invasive route: an accessible peripheral lymph node, CT-guided biopsy, or bronchoscopic and endobronchial ultrasound sampling. Pleural fluid cytology if there is an effusion.
Tumour markers for a young patient with an anterior mediastinal mass (AFP, beta-hCG) and LDH.
Flow-volume loop or awake airway assessment before any anaesthetic, decided with the anaesthetist.

resuscitate.text: Corticosteroids are reserved for airway oedema or steroid-responsive tumours once tissue is secured, or when the airway cannot wait.
Anticoagulation when the cause is thrombosis, including catheter-related, after discussion of bleeding risk.
Avoid sedation and supine positioning in a symptomatic patient with a mediastinal mass until an airway plan exists.

definitive.text: Endovenous stent for symptomatic obstruction gives the quickest relief and does not compromise later histology; it is offered for symptom relief in lung cancer.
Treat the cause once the histology is known: chemotherapy for chemosensitive tumours such as small cell lung cancer, lymphoma and germ cell tumours, and radiotherapy where appropriate.

Surgical bypass or resection of the SVC is rarely indicated: for benign causes refractory to endovascular treatment, or as part of resection of a selected thymoma or lung cancer in a specialist thoracic unit.

escalate.text: Oncology and interventional radiology the same day for severe symptoms.
Senior anaesthetist before any biopsy under anaesthesia; cardiothoracic surgery if cardiopulmonary bypass standby is being considered for a critical mediastinal mass.
Critical care for airway compromise or cerebral oedema.

notes: SVCO is rarely an emergency in itself: the collateral circulation buys days. The real emergencies are the airway and the brain.
The surgeon is most often asked for a biopsy. The best contribution is choosing the safest route to tissue, often not a general anaesthetic.
Steroids given 'just in case' can cost the patient a diagnosis of lymphoma. Ask whether the airway truly cannot wait.
